I am 75 years old, and I have worked this same 3 mu of land in Quzhou for 50 years. I live alone, so every decision I make has to balance what the crop needs against what my back and my schedule can handle. Cotton is the only crop I grow — it is what this soil knows, and it is what I know. This spring, when the soil warms up in late April, I will sow improved cotton seeds. I stopped using traditional seeds years ago because the improved varieties give heavier bolls and hold up better against pests. I will prepare the field with rotary tillage. It is less exhausting than ploughing, and at my age I need to conserve my strength. For fertilizer, I will apply 15 kg of nitrogen per mu, 5 kg of phosphorus, and 6 kg of potassium. I have learned that this land needs a little more potassium now than it did thirty years ago to keep the bolls from dropping early. I will split the nitrogen — half at sowing and half at flowering — so the plants get food when they need it most. I will irrigate three times from my well: once right after sowing to settle the seeds, once at flowering when the plants are thirsty, and once during boll formation. Three times is enough to keep the yield without wearing me out running the pump every week. For pests, I will spray four times. I watch the leaves every morning, and with 50 years of looking at cotton plants I know when the bollworms and aphids are coming before they do real damage. I expect about 90 kg of seed cotton per mu this year. That gives me roughly 270 kg in total, which will cover my costs and leave enough for me to live on through the winter.
